vitamin-a.title: Vitamin A
vitamin-a.description: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin that is naturally present in many foods. Vitamin A is important for normal vision, the immune system, reproduction, and growth and development. Vitamin A also helps your heart, lungs, and other organs work properly. Carotenoids are pigments that give yellow, orange, and red fruits and vegetables their color. Your body is able to convert some carotenoids into vitamin A.
vitamin-a.keyFunctionsHtml:
Vitamin A is essential for normal vision, immune function, reproduction, growth, and development. It helps maintain the normal structure and function of the eyes, heart, lungs, and other organs.

  • Vision: Vitamin A is needed to see in low light and to maintain normal eye function.
  • Immune system: It supports the body's ability to fight infections.
  • Growth and development: It contributes to normal cell growth and development.
  • Reproduction: It plays a role in normal reproductive function.
  • Organ health: It helps maintain the normal function of the heart, lungs, and other organs.

Vitamin A comes from two main dietary sources: preformed vitamin A, found in animal-derived foods, and provitamin A carotenoids, found in plant foods. The body converts some carotenoids, especially beta-carotene, into vitamin A.
vitamin-a.foodSourcesHtml:
Vitamin A is naturally present in many foods and is also added to some fortified foods. Good dietary sources include:

  • Fish: Certain types of fish, including herring and salmon.
  • Organ meats: Beef liver and other organ meats, which can contain very high amounts of vitamin A.
  • Vegetables: Carrots, sweet potatoes, spinach, broccoli, and winter squash, particularly green leafy and orange or yellow vegetables.
  • Fruits: Mangoes, apricots, and cantaloupe.
  • Dairy products: Milk and cheese.
  • Other foods: Eggs and breakfast cereals fortified with vitamin A.

Animal foods generally provide preformed vitamin A, while many colorful fruits and vegetables provide provitamin A carotenoids that the body can convert into vitamin A. Eating a varied diet can help meet daily needs. Liver should be consumed in moderation because it can contain very high amounts of vitamin A.
vitamin-a.deficiencyHtml:
Vitamin A deficiency occurs when the body does not receive or absorb enough vitamin A. It is uncommon in populations with adequate access to a varied diet but remains a significant public health problem in some countries, particularly among young children.

Possible consequences of deficiency include:

  • Night blindness: Difficulty seeing in dim light or darkness; this is one of the earliest and most common signs.
  • Xerophthalmia: An eye condition that can damage the cornea and lead to permanent blindness if left untreated.
  • Increased susceptibility to infections: Deficiency can increase the risk or severity of infections, including respiratory infections, measles, and diarrhea.
  • Anemia: Long-term deficiency can contribute to anemia.
  • Impaired growth and development: Insufficient vitamin A can adversely affect normal development, especially in children.

People at increased risk include premature infants, young children and pregnant or breastfeeding people in populations with limited access to vitamin A-rich foods, as well as people with conditions that impair nutrient absorption, such as cystic fibrosis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or celiac disease.

Persistent vision problems or suspected deficiency require medical evaluation. High-dose vitamin A supplements should not be used to treat deficiency without appropriate medical guidance.
vitamin-a.overdoseHtml:
Excessive intake of preformed vitamin A can be harmful because this fat-soluble vitamin is stored in the body, mainly in the liver, and can accumulate over time. Toxicity most often results from high-dose supplements or certain medicines rather than from eating a varied diet.

Symptoms of excessive preformed vitamin A may include:

  • Severe headache and blurred vision.
  • Nausea and dizziness.
  • Muscle aches and problems with coordination.
  • With prolonged excessive intake, dry skin, painful muscles and joints, fatigue, and liver problems.
  • In severe cases, increased pressure around the brain, coma, or death.

Pregnancy: Excessive preformed vitamin A can cause serious birth defects, including abnormalities affecting the eyes, skull, lungs, and heart. People who are pregnant, may become pregnant, or are breastfeeding should avoid high-dose preformed vitamin A supplements unless specifically directed by a healthcare professional.

Beta-carotene: High intake can cause a harmless yellow-orange discoloration of the skin. However, high-dose beta-carotene supplements have been associated with an increased risk of lung cancer and death in smokers, former smokers, and people exposed to asbestos.

Upper intake limits for preformed vitamin A from all sources:

  • Birth to 12 months: 600 mcg per day.
  • Children 1–3 years: 600 mcg per day.
  • Children 4–8 years: 900 mcg per day.
  • Children 9–13 years: 1,700 mcg per day.
  • Adolescents 14–18 years: 2,800 mcg per day.
  • Adults 19 years and older: 3,000 mcg per day.

These limits apply to preformed vitamin A, not beta-carotene or other provitamin A carotenoids. They do not apply to medically supervised treatment. Consult a healthcare professional before taking high-dose vitamin A supplements, particularly during pregnancy or when using medicines that may interact with vitamin A.
